title: Gavin Volure

jokes.text: I'm in connecticut, i haven't eaten, and i'm stressed about an 'away toilet' situation.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Liz to loosen up at the party.
jokes.punchline: Liz's list of grievances culminates in the absurdly specific and overly personal 'away toilet' situation — the joke is that this is her real source of anxiety.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Liz Lemon — the escalating list of complaints ending in a euphemism for bathroom anxiety is sharp character comedy. 'Away toilet' is a specific, original coinage that only she would use. High character integration.

jokes.text: He was the first man to be on the cover of Fortune and Jet magazine at the same time. Of course, that was back when Jet was actually about jet ownership.
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining Gavin Volure's prestige by referencing his Fortune and Jet magazine covers.
jokes.punchline: The absurd clarification that Jet magazine used to be about literal jet ownership — a completely fabricated and deadpan rewrite of the magazine's history.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. The misdirection is elegant — you expect a racial joke (Jet is famously a Black magazine) but instead the show pivots to an absurdist alternate history of the magazine being about actual jets, which is both funnier and more original. Perfect economy. Very 30 Rock.

jokes.text: That magazine took a weird turn. / These are not chips.
jokes.setup: Jack just made the Jet magazine joke. Liz has been eating what she thought were chips.
jokes.punchline: Two simultaneous reactions: Jack's dry understatement about the magazine pivot, and Liz's matter-of-fact announcement that the potpourri she was eating isn't chips.
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff on the potpourri gag is well-timed and the deadpan delivery implied by 'These are not chips' (not a scream, just a statement) is great character work. Jack's line functions as a dry button on his own joke.

jokes.text: They say he hasn't left his home in almost three years. / Well, I hope he shows up for dinner. / He's already here.
jokes.setup: Jack explains Volure hasn't left his home in three years, and Liz naively asks if he'll show up to dinner.
jokes.punchline: Gavin's simple, flat 'He's already here' — the joke is Liz's obliviousness to an obvious implication.
jokes.explanation: A clean, well-structured classic setup/punchline. The comedy comes from Liz's failure to connect the obvious dots. Good economy. Not especially original but executes efficiently.

jokes.text: Because of my severe agoraphobia and my debilitating wealth...
jokes.setup: Gavin is explaining why he hosts dinners at his home.
jokes.punchline: Pairing 'severe agoraphobia' with 'debilitating wealth' — treating extreme wealth as an affliction comparable to a mental disorder.
jokes.explanation: 'Debilitating wealth' is an excellent original coinage — treating obscene wealth as a disability is a sharp satirical move with perfect economy. Character-specific for this eccentric billionaire archetype.

jokes.text: The world of fashion, society, art collecting and yelling — Why isn't there any good art in here? Come on!
jokes.setup: Gavin lists the diverse 'walks of life' at his dinner: fashion, society, art collecting, and...
jokes.punchline: Mid-sentence, an off-screen voice yells exactly the kind of thing that 'yelling' as a category implies — immediately demonstrating what it means.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the structural simultaneity — Gavin names 'yelling' as a category just as someone yells. The immediate illustration is very well-timed and the absurd categorization of 'yelling' as a social identity is clever.

jokes.text: What if the Germans had won the war, Lemon? / Business and historical fiction.
jokes.setup: Gavin lists guests from 'business and historical fiction.' Someone yells a question about WWII.
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition reveals the 'historical fiction' guest is a Hitler-wins alternate-history obsessive.
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist character sketch — the alt-history fiction obsessive is a recognizable type. Competent but not deeply original.

jokes.text: Funny story, I was only wearing that because the fire alarm went off while I was getting a haircut.
jokes.setup: Gavin says Liz looked beautiful in her photo in the NYT Style section.
jokes.punchline: Liz deflects the compliment by explaining the photo was an accident during a haircut fire alarm — implying her actual style is not photo-worthy.
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz Lemon deflection of a compliment with a self-deprecating explanation. High character integration — only Liz would tell this story unprompted. The specific detail (mid-haircut) adds texture.

jokes.text: I keep one chair empty to represent our unfulfilled hopes and dreams. / I'm just kidding, Eliot Spitzer's hooker couldn't make it.
jokes.setup: Gavin solemnly announces one empty chair represents 'unfulfilled hopes and dreams.'
jokes.punchline: Immediate puncture: the chair was for Eliot Spitzer's (then-current-scandal) prostitute who canceled.
jokes.explanation: Textbook misdirection: the setup is genuinely elegant (the empty chair metaphor is beautiful), making the deflation into a topical sex scandal joke extremely funny. The structure is near-perfect — the pretense is fully committed before the punchline arrives.

jokes.text: 77th and Amsterdam, 68th and Columbus, 125th and President Clinton Boulevard. Also don't overthink it, Sara Lee, frozen, unbelievable.
jokes.setup: Gavin asks if anyone knows a good place for cupcakes in Manhattan.
jokes.punchline: A guest rattles off several legitimate addresses, then the surprise pivot to 'Sara Lee, frozen, unbelievable' — undercut by someone being identified as McEnroe (implying John McEnroe is a cupcake connoisseur).
jokes.explanation: The list structure builds through legitimate answers and lands on the absurdist anti-punchline of frozen Sara Lee. The 'McEnroe, give me a break' name-drop adds an extra layer. Good escalation structure.

jokes.text: Also, don't overthink it, Sara Lee, frozen, unbelievable.
jokes.setup: McEnroe has rattled off a list of upscale Manhattan cupcake locations.
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts his own sophisticated list by recommending frozen Sara Lee as equally valid, delivered with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: The deflation from upscale Manhattan cupcakeries to frozen supermarket cake is a solid joke. The rhythm — the staccato comma-separated recommendation — is well-executed. 'Unbelievable' as the closer is a good button.

jokes.text: You know my two sons, Tracy Jr. and George Foreman? They've been acting really weird lately. / Where you going? / Nowhere.
jokes.setup: Tracy tells Kenneth his sons have been acting weird, then we cut to Tracy's sons.
jokes.punchline: The sons' suspicious, guilty 'Nowhere' — immediately confirming Tracy's fears.
jokes.explanation: A setup for the Menendez Brothers running gag. The name 'George Foreman' for a son is an absurdist bonus. The cut to the suspicious sons is competent but predictable.

jokes.text: Those two have never paid me any attention. And rightly so. I'm a strange man who can't be taken seriously.
jokes.setup: Tracy complains his sons are suddenly paying him too much attention.
jokes.punchline: 'And rightly so' — Tracy agrees with his own dismissal, then elaborates with self-aware absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's self-awareness deployed in a completely unexpected direction — agreeing he shouldn't be taken seriously is both funny and oddly touching. High character integration; this joke only works for Tracy.

jokes.text: Look what the little one made me. / Aw, that's cute. / This is voodoo, Ken!
jokes.setup: Kenneth sees what Tracy's son made and calls it cute.
jokes.punchline: Tracy reveals it's a voodoo doll — Kenneth sees art, Tracy sees a death threat.
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of the voodoo doll being mistaken for cute child art is a solid misdirect. Tracy's paranoid certainty sells it. The 'This is voodoo, Ken!' delivery is a strong character moment.

jokes.text: I know I was a handful when my family moved from our farmhouse to that militia camp in the woods.
jokes.setup: Kenneth suggests kids act out when there are big changes, drawing on his own childhood.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'farmhouse' to 'militia camp in the woods' as a matter-of-fact family relocation.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. The joke deepens our understanding of Kenneth's disturbing rural background while being completely in his voice — he delivers it as a normal comparison. 'Militia camp in the woods' is a brilliant specific detail. High rewatch value as it builds Kenneth's mythology.

jokes.text: The life-sized Tracy Jordan sex doll. They're selling like hotcakes in Japan.
jokes.setup: Tracy lists the various revenue streams from his success: video games, tie-ins, toys...
jokes.punchline: The sex doll as a legitimate merchandise item, with the Japan specification adding a layer of absurdist specificity.
jokes.explanation: The sex doll is introduced here and pays off repeatedly throughout the episode. As a setup it's doing heavy lifting. The Japan detail elevates it from basic absurdism to something more specifically funny. Rewatch bonus for what follows.

jokes.text: Well, you know what they say, money is the root of all evil. / I thought that was just a tagline for my movie, Death Bank.
jokes.setup: Kenneth uses the common saying about money being the root of all evil.
jokes.punchline: Tracy genuinely believed that was an original tagline from his movie 'Death Bank' — revealing both his ignorance and the existence of a film called Death Bank.
jokes.explanation: Sharp character joke — Tracy's obliviousness to common cultural knowledge expressed through the lens of his absurd film career. 'Death Bank' as a movie title is perfect. The sincerity of his confusion makes it land.

jokes.text: It's like Picasso not painting, or Bruce Willis not combining action and rock harmonica.
jokes.setup: Jack flatters Volure that he shouldn't be 'out of the game.'
jokes.punchline: Pairing Picasso with Bruce Willis as equivalently legendary figures, with 'rock harmonica' as Willis's defining artistic contribution.
jokes.explanation: 'Rock harmonica' is a wonderfully specific and absurd detail — Bruce Willis's harmonica playing is real but incredibly obscure, and treating it as his primary artistic legacy alongside Picasso is both inside-baseball and perfectly timed. Jack's earnestness sells it.

jokes.text: Wind power, bandwidth, Chinese market. / Oh, god.
jokes.setup: Gavin pitches his new company to Jack.
jokes.punchline: The pitch is three buzzwords with no actual content, and Liz's deflated 'Oh, god' acknowledges the absurdity while Jack (presumably) is riveted.
jokes.explanation: Sharp satire of empty tech/business pitching — three buzzwords that mean nothing together. Liz's reaction grounds it. Jack's presumably visible excitement makes this a three-way comedy beat.

jokes.text: This is the most exciting day of my life. And I was pulled onstage once to dance at a Bruce Springsteen concert.
jokes.setup: Jack expresses extreme excitement about Volure's investment opportunity.
jokes.punchline: The comparison to being pulled onstage at a Springsteen concert — the specificity of this as Jack's personal benchmark for excitement is perfectly character-revealing.
jokes.explanation: Jack's unexpected vulnerability/enthusiasm expressed through a very human Springsteen memory is great character work. The specificity ('pulled onstage to dance') creates a vivid, funny image of patrician Jack Donaghy doing exactly that.

jokes.text: Just think, this time next year, you'll be so rich you can run for political office without having to pretend to be a fundamentalist.
jokes.setup: Jack welcomes Volure 'aboard' the investment.
jokes.punchline: The casually cynical implication that political ambition requires faking religious fundamentalism — delivered as a selling point.
jokes.explanation: Sharp political satire delivered as a throwaway benefit. Only Jack would frame fake religious fundamentalism as an inconvenience of insufficient wealth. Very much his character's worldview encapsulated in one line.

jokes.text: Because my agoraphobia-related germ issues prevent direct human contact, I wonder if Carl here might say good night to you for me? Carl? / Good night, Liz. I hope to see you again soon.
jokes.setup: Gavin wants to say a proper goodbye to Liz but claims germ issues prevent contact.
jokes.punchline: He has his 'driver' Carl physically say goodbye on his behalf — a deeply strange proxy goodbye that Liz accepts.
jokes.explanation: Absurdist and structurally elegant — the proxy goodbye is a novel comedic concept, and it pays off later when Carl is revealed to be a U.S. Marshal. The visual of Carl earnestly delivering Gavin's farewell while Liz awkwardly accepts it is rich. High rewatch value.

jokes.text: Terrorist attacks, Cloverfield monsters. I can't do it, because my head is too big for the helmet.
jokes.setup: Liz announces the floor needs an emergency marshal for various threats.
jokes.punchline: She can't do it herself because her head is too big for the emergency helmet — treating this as a disqualifying medical condition.
jokes.explanation: Two jokes layered: 'Cloverfield monsters' as a legitimate emergency category (absurdist topical joke about the recent film), and the self-deprecating large-head disclosure. Both are quick and economical.

jokes.text: No, but you have a big head. / That's not a burn, I just said that.
jokes.setup: Someone points out Liz has a big head after she disclosed it.
jokes.punchline: Liz clarifies it wasn't an insult — she was just stating a fact — which is somehow funnier than if it were intended as a burn.
jokes.explanation: The meta-deflation of the burn structure is clever — refusing to let it be an insult makes it somehow more insulting. Good economy and a sharp structural subversion of the 'that's a burn' joke format.

jokes.text: Cerie, is my phone ringing? / It is. Wow, you have, like, dog ears. / So are you going to... Okay.
jokes.setup: Liz asks if her phone is ringing across the room.
jokes.punchline: Cerie compliments Liz's 'dog ears' for hearing it, then trails off instead of answering the phone — leaving Liz to handle it herself.
jokes.explanation: A reliable Cerie joke — she's oblivious and unhelpful in a bubbly way. 'Dog ears' is a sweet but useless compliment. The trailing 'So are you going to... Okay' is a nice awkward reaction beat. Competent character comedy.

jokes.text: Well... This must be what the kids call 'a booty call.' / I haven't been out of the house since 2004, and even I know the kids don't call it that anymore.
jokes.setup: Gavin asks Liz out privately (not a party), and Liz tries to use slang to characterize it.
jokes.punchline: Gavin — a recluse since 2004 — is more current on slang than Liz, which says everything about how uncool Liz is.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured. The twist is that an agoraphobic recluse who hasn't left home since 2004 is somehow MORE culturally current than Liz. This is devastating character comedy for Liz and a great use of Gavin's established trait. Economy and character integration are both near-perfect.

jokes.text: I'll send a helicopter to take you to the train station.
jokes.setup: Gavin confirms the date and Liz agrees.
jokes.punchline: The ludicrous over-the-top transportation offer (helicopter to a train station) reveals the scale of his wealth/eccentricity.
jokes.explanation: The bathos of helicopter-to-train-station is a nice reversal of expected luxury escalation. Efficient character establishment joke.

jokes.text: What the what?
jokes.setup: Liz has just been invited on a date by a billionaire who offered her a helicopter.
jokes.punchline: Her signature catchphrase reaction — a self-censored 'what the f***' — which is perfectly Liz: too proper to swear, too confused not to react.
jokes.explanation: A running gag/catchphrase for Liz. High quotability and character integration. The joke is entirely in the delivery and the specific Liz Lemon self-censorship. Not deeply crafted but perfectly deployed.

jokes.text: Tracy watching the Menendez Brothers documentary and slowly realizing his sons might kill him for his money.
jokes.setup: Tracy is watching a true crime documentary about the Menendez brothers murdering their father for money.
jokes.punchline: 'My kids are going to kill me!' — Tracy's paranoid leap from TV documentary to his own situation.
jokes.explanation: The Menendez Brothers parody is the episode's B-plot engine. The moment Tracy connects the documentary to his life is a strong visual/reaction beat. His immediate certainty is character-perfect.

jokes.text: I just don't let myself read the t-shirts with off-color slogans.
jokes.setup: Kenneth explains he's taking in laundry for extra money.
jokes.punchline: His self-imposed rule about off-color t-shirt slogans reveals his sheltered innocence while suggesting he's encountered them anyway.
jokes.explanation: Small but perfectly formed Kenneth character moment. The detail does a lot of work in establishing his prudishness while being oddly specific and therefore funny. 'Don't let myself read' implies effort.

jokes.text: I know we pay you a living wage, I fought against it.
jokes.setup: Jack acknowledges Kenneth earns a living wage.
jokes.punchline: 'I fought against it' — a throwaway confession of Jack's labor politics delivered with zero shame.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Devastating economy — five words reveal Jack's entire class politics. The casual confession of fighting against a living wage, delivered as a neutral aside, is a perfect Jack Donaghy joke. Only Jack could deliver this with such complete lack of self-consciousness.

jokes.text: After years of inbreeding, the pigs are getting violent. And the pig shield around the house has worn thin.
jokes.setup: Kenneth explains why he needs to send more money home to the farm.
jokes.punchline: 'Pig shield' — as if this is a standard piece of rural home infrastructure.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding Kenneth worldbuilding. 'Pig shield' is an inspired coinage — it implies a specific piece of rural architecture that no one else would have. The combination of inbreeding + pig violence + structural pig defense is escalating absurdism delivered in Kenneth's matter-of-fact register. Among the episode's best.

jokes.text: If you don't include Confederate money? / 4000.
jokes.setup: Jack asks how much money Kenneth has in savings.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's qualification that the total depends on whether you count Confederate money — implying he has Confederate money in his savings.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Kenneth character joke. His instinct to qualify the Confederate money — not to hide it but because it might affect the math — is hilariously specific to his Southern, militia-adjacent background. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: After I invest this money, you'll be able to buy your folks a pig moat.
jokes.setup: Jack is moved to invest Kenneth's money as a gesture of goodwill.
jokes.punchline: Jack proposes a 'pig moat' as an upgrade from the pig shield — both taking the pig crisis seriously AND suggesting an absurd medieval solution.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback — Jack engages completely sincerely with the pig problem and proposes a moat, which is both medieval and logical. The fact that Jack Donaghy, patrician GE executive, is earnestly discussing pig moats is inherently funny. Great economy.

jokes.text: Well, that would be great if pigs weren't excellent swimmers.
jokes.setup: Jack suggests a pig moat as the solution to the violent pig problem.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's practical objection — pigs are excellent swimmers — delivered with the gravity of real expertise.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke by structure. The pig moat is proposed as a genuine solution, and Kenneth's perfectly deadpan factual refutation ('pigs are excellent swimmers') demolishes it completely while expanding the absurdist mythology. The callback chain — pig shield → pig moat → swimming pigs — is a miniature masterclass in escalating absurdism. Exceptional economy and character integration. This is what a 9 looks like.

jokes.text: I thought he might. He asked if we were involved, I said you used to have a thing for me, but you were getting over it. / That is what's happening, right?
jokes.setup: Liz says Gavin called and asked her out. Jack says he 'thought he might.'
jokes.punchline: Jack reveals he told Gavin that Liz had a thing for Jack but was 'getting over it' — and then earnestly checks if that's accurate.
jokes.explanation: Jack's breezy management of Liz's romantic life, combined with his genuine uncertainty about whether Liz does have a thing for him, is great character comedy. The 'That is what's happening, right?' check is perfectly Jack — arrogant enough to believe it's true.

jokes.text: All the nodding and smiling and sibling listing. And what's the upside? It works and you have to have a bunch of sex?
jokes.setup: Liz complains about the exhaustion of getting to know someone new.
jokes.punchline: The 'upside' of a relationship working is framed as a burden: having to have 'a bunch of sex.' Only Liz would frame sexual success as a downside.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Liz Lemon character comedy. 'Sibling listing' as a specific exhausting first-date ritual is a sharp observational detail, and the pivot to sex-as-burden is both funny and deeply revealing of her character. High character integration.

jokes.text: No, I just wish I could start a relationship about 12 years in, when you really don't have to try anymore and you can just sit around together and goof on TV shows, and then go to bed without anybody trying any funny business.
jokes.setup: Jack asks if Liz wants to be alone for the rest of her life.
jokes.punchline: Liz's ideal relationship is a loveless, sexless, comfortable middle-aged companionship — 12 years in, no effort, no 'funny business.'
jokes.explanation: One of the great Liz Lemon monologues. 'Start a relationship 12 years in' is a perfectly articulated anti-romantic fantasy that is both extremely funny and heartbreakingly accurate to the character. High quotability. 'Funny business' as an old-fashioned euphemism for sex is a perfect Liz word choice.

jokes.text: If I were dating a man, he would be the top of my list with Michael Jordan, Denzel Washington, Taye Diggs... God, do I have a Black thing?
jokes.setup: Jack endorses Gavin Volure as a dating prospect.
jokes.punchline: Jack lists his 'men I'd date' top three — all Black celebrities — and has a moment of self-realization about this pattern.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Jack's oblivious self-examination is a recurring type for the show. The specificity of the list (Jordan, Washington, Diggs) and the genuine bewilderment at his own taste is funny. The 'do I have a Black thing?' question is treated as a genuine mystery rather than a punchline.

jokes.text: Lemon, you're going to go to Gavin's, and you're going to work this thing like a Chinese gymnast. Wear something tight, force a smile, and lie about your age.
jokes.setup: Jack is coaching Liz on how to approach her date.
jokes.punchline: The 'Chinese gymnast' metaphor yields the specific instructions: wear something tight, force a smile, lie about your age — all of which are both good relationship advice and specifically applicable to Chinese Olympic gymnasts.
jokes.explanation: The metaphor is richly constructed — the Chinese gymnast analogy works on two levels simultaneously (dating strategy and Olympic performance), and the three specific instructions all fit both contexts perfectly. Sharp writing.

jokes.text: Daddy's home. / Don't Menendez me.
jokes.setup: Tracy comes home and his son greets him.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's pre-emptive 'Don't Menendez me' — treating a normal greeting with murderous suspicion.
jokes.explanation: 'Don't Menendez me' is a brilliant neologism — turning the Menendez Brothers into a verb meaning 'patricide.' Economy is exceptional. High quotability. The absurdity of using this as a casual family greeting is perfect.

jokes.text: We made the hockey team.
jokes.setup: Tracy is visibly paranoid and suspicious of his sons' normal behavior.
jokes.punchline: The sons' completely innocent announcement — they made the hockey team — lands as absurdly mundane against Tracy's murder paranoia.
jokes.explanation: The anticlimax of the hockey team announcement works as a beat deflating Tracy's paranoia. Simple but effective structure. The joke is mostly in the contrast.

jokes.text: One of these benches is a priceless work of art, and the other is an ordinary bench from which to admire it. Which one's which?
jokes.setup: Gavin is giving Liz a tour of his home.
jokes.punchline: The philosophical puzzle of art vs. function is presented sincerely, and the invitation to guess highlights both the pretension of modern art and Gavin's eccentricity.
jokes.explanation: A compact, well-executed absurdist joke about modern art pretension. The deadpan presentation of an unanswerable art question is characterful and economical.

jokes.text: I'd be lying if I told you I never danced with a broom. / That's nothing, sometimes, to feel like I have company during dinner, I dispute credit card charges on speaker phone.
jokes.setup: Gavin admits to lonely eccentric behavior (dancing with a broom) to show Liz his vulnerability.
jokes.punchline: Liz one-ups him with her own loneliness hack — disputing credit card charges on speaker phone for the company-like experience.
jokes.explanation: The episode's comedic peak. The credit card disputes-as-social-interaction joke is staggeringly original — it takes Liz's loneliness to a new, specific, and completely credible place. Only Liz Lemon would find this hack, and the way it one-ups a billionaire's broom-dancing is structurally perfect escalation. Immediately quotable and iconic. This is a strong 9.

jokes.text: We can never leave the house, and we'd just probably sit around all weekend and watch TV. / Go on. / There's not much else to do but eat, read celebrity gossip on the internet, and nap the day away. / Really? / And unfortunately, because of my phobias, we could never be physically intimate.
jokes.setup: Gavin warns Liz that his agoraphobia makes a relationship difficult.
jokes.punchline: Each 'limitation' he lists (TV, eating, celebrity gossip, napping, no sex) is received by Liz with increasing enthusiasm — her ideal relationship is exactly what he's describing.
jokes.explanation: A masterful callback to Liz's '12 years in' speech — everything she described as ideal is precisely what Gavin is offering as a warning. The escalating 'Go on' and 'Really?' reactions are pitch-perfect. The punchline of no physical intimacy being the final selling point is earned and devastating. One of the episode's top three moments.

jokes.text: Kenneth, I'm very proud of you. Next stop, home ownership. / I'm just kidding. The middle class is dying, you'll be renting forever.
jokes.setup: Jack praises Kenneth for street performing to earn investment money.
jokes.punchline: After the inspiring 'next stop, home ownership,' Jack immediately undercuts it with the honest economic forecast.
jokes.explanation: Another textbook Jack Donaghy moment — the encouragement immediately retracted in favor of bleak economic realism. 'The middle class is dying, you'll be renting forever' is a punch disguised as candor. High character integration and economy.

jokes.text: You'd have been better off putting that money in a coffee can.
jokes.setup: Jack's broker reveals the investment account has been completely emptied.
jokes.punchline: The broker's dry advisory that a coffee can would have been a superior financial instrument.
jokes.explanation: A functional, competent joke but not particularly original. The coffee can as a better investment than a fraud scheme is a well-worn comic image. Gets the scene's comic work done efficiently.

jokes.text: Hi, Walter. This is Kenneth Parcell, NBC page program. What's the status of MY investment?
jokes.setup: Jack has just gotten bad news about the investment from his broker.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth, having overheard, confidently and formally introduces himself to the broker by title and asks his own question — the contrast between his small savings and Jack's institutional investment being treated identically is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's formal self-identification as 'NBC page program' followed by his proprietary 'MY investment' question is a delight. His earnestness in treating his $4,000 with the same gravity as Jack's millions is perfect character work.

jokes.text: Yeah. They can't seem to get anything right up there, can they?
jokes.setup: Liz enjoyed watching MTV Canada with Gavin.
jokes.punchline: Gavin's smug dismissal of Canadian television — ironic given he's a fraud under house arrest.
jokes.explanation: A minor joke, functional. The irony of a house-arrested fraudster dismissing Canadian competence is a light touch. Not especially original.

jokes.text: Look, Liz, I've decided I can trust you, so I'm going to tell you the truth. I'm not really an eccentric agoraphobe. I just tell people that so they won't know I'm under house arrest for tax fraud. / And arson.
jokes.setup: Gavin says he's going to tell Liz the 'truth' about his agoraphobia.
jokes.punchline: The 'and arson' addition as a casual afterthought — tax fraud feels manageable, but arson significantly upgrades the threat.
jokes.explanation: The 'and arson' beat is a classic escalation structure — the second charge always being worse than the first, dropped in as if it's a minor addendum. Well-timed and economical.

jokes.text: I thought Derek was upstairs. / I miscounted the men, Liz! I miscounted the men!
jokes.setup: Gavin is trying to escape while avoiding the U.S. Marshals guarding him.
jokes.punchline: 'I miscounted the men' — the absurdly military phrasing from a white-collar criminal who clearly has been planning this escape with tactical seriousness.
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'I miscounted the men!' is both panic-funny and the show's most quoted moment from this episode. The phrase has a military gravity absurdly misapplied to a white-collar criminal's household escape plan. The doubled delivery sells it perfectly.

jokes.text: Also that joke answering machine message makes me really think you've picked up, so I start talking, and then it beeps, and, uh, I feel like a fool.
jokes.setup: Jack leaves an urgent voicemail for Gavin.
jokes.punchline: After his urgent business message, Jack adds a complaint about Gavin's tricky answering machine greeting — a very human, relatable frustration incongruously voiced by Jack Donaghy.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Jack's urgent crisis message with his petty voicemail-etiquette complaint is very funny. The vulnerability ('I feel like a fool') is unexpected from Jack and lands well. A small moment with good character specificity.

jokes.text: And he's not a germaphobe! I thought I was helping him when I let him hold my boob while we watched Top Chef.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Liz that Gavin is a crook and not actually a germaphobe.
jokes.punchline: Liz's revelation that she accommodated what she thought was a medical need by allowing him to hold her breast during a cooking show.
jokes.explanation: An outstanding joke. The callback to the germaphobe setup pays off in the most unexpected and perfect way — Liz's charitable misreading of a perverted act as a medical accommodation is both hilarious and completely in character. 'While we watched Top Chef' is the perfect mundane detail. High quotability. The show's second-best joke.

jokes.text: I'm going to hit Gavin Volure harder than a bottle of whiskey in an Irish wake.
jokes.setup: Jack promises to fix the situation and take revenge on Volure.
jokes.punchline: The threat is expressed as a vivid simile — hitting him harder than a bottle of whiskey at an Irish wake (i.e., very hard and very fast).
jokes.explanation: A colorful Jack-ism that plays on his WASP background making an Irish reference feel slightly foreign and therefore funnier. The simile is vivid and economical, if not exceptional.

jokes.text: Tracy, get out of the hallway. / Or am I? / Oh god, this dream again? / That's not me. That's the Tracy Jordan Japanese sex doll. You can tell us apart because it's not suffering from a vitamin deficiency.
jokes.setup: Liz finds Tracy (or seemingly Tracy) in the hallway.
jokes.punchline: Tracy reveals it's his sex doll in the hallway, and the way to distinguish them is that the doll doesn't have Tracy's vitamin deficiency.
jokes.explanation: The sex doll callback pays off beautifully. 'You can tell us apart because it's not suffering from a vitamin deficiency' is a great line — the distinguishing characteristic being the doll's better health is unexpected and characterful. 'Or am I?' before the reveal is a perfect beat.

jokes.text: Other than the natural inclination to make love to yourself, why did you get this? / To use as a decoy. So my greedy children will murder it, and I'll be able to escape un-Mendezed.
jokes.setup: Liz asks why Tracy has his own sex doll.
jokes.punchline: The elaborate murder decoy plan — using the sex doll to absorb a patricide attempt while he escapes — is revealed as Tracy's solution.
jokes.explanation: Excellent convergence of two running gags — the sex doll and the Menendez Brothers paranoia. The plan is both absurd and internally logical for Tracy. 'Un-Mendezed' as a verb is a great coinage.

jokes.text: The parallels between the Jordans and the Mendezis are uncanny. Both families are rich, both families have two sons, and both families are staples of Court TV.
jokes.setup: Tracy argues the Menendez Brothers situation mirrors his own family.
jokes.punchline: His third 'parallel' — 'both families are staples of Court TV' — is self-incriminating and presented as if it's a coincidence rather than evidence of his own legal history.
jokes.explanation: The list structure escalates to the self-incriminating Court TV detail, which Tracy is seemingly unaware implicates him. His earnest parallel-drawing reveals his own legal troubles. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Sorry, Jack, but I needed that money for my escape. And it's all gone. I spent it on disguises.
jokes.setup: Jack confronts Gavin about stealing the investment money.
jokes.punchline: He spent their investment money on 'disguises' — an absurdly low-priority use of funds for an elaborate white-collar escape plan.
jokes.explanation: The bathos of a billionaire scheme collapsing because the money went to costumes is funny. The word 'disguises' does most of the work — very specific and slightly childish. Competent.

jokes.text: You watch our commercials, we never actually say what we did. / INNOVATION / TOMORROW / AMERICA / SUNSTREAM
jokes.setup: Jack demands to know about Sunstream, the company that supposedly made Gavin billions.
jokes.punchline: Gavin reveals it's a fake company whose commercials consist entirely of inspirational buzzwords — and we see/hear the actual commercial, which is exactly that.
jokes.explanation: Sharp satire of hollow corporate branding that feels timeless. The commercial parody — four single words — is the joke in its purest form. The visual of the commercial playing as evidence is a great structural choice. Very quotable format.

jokes.text: I share with three other white collar criminals. / Hey, Glenn, that's my peanut butter. / Creamy? This is — this is not my peanut — I'm sorry, Glenn.
jokes.setup: Gavin reveals the government owns the house and he shares it with other white-collar criminals.
jokes.punchline: The white-collar criminal communal living is immediately illustrated by a petty peanut butter dispute — the banality of their shared domestic life.
jokes.explanation: The peanut butter dispute grounds the absurd white-collar criminal commune in mundane reality. Gavin's immediate capitulation to Glenn ('I'm sorry, Glenn') reveals his reduced status perfectly. Good character deflation.

jokes.text: Damn it. I have got a serious case of the Mondays.
jokes.setup: Jack is moved while listening to Gavin miss Liz, then catches himself.
jokes.punchline: Jack deflects his genuine emotion with the office cliché 'case of the Mondays' — absurd in this context because (a) it's a meaningless deflection and (b) Jack Donaghy using this phrase is inherently wrong.
jokes.explanation: Jack Donaghy using a 'case of the Mondays' to disguise genuine human feeling is a great character moment. The phrase is so wrong for him that it becomes funny. The Office Space reference adds a layer for savvy viewers.

jokes.text: We trusted you, Gavin. / I know, good point. / And you betrayed us. / Wow, that's wonderful news.
jokes.setup: Jack tries to guilt Gavin into making things right.
jokes.punchline: Gavin's responses are completely disconnected from what Jack is saying — he agrees with 'betrayal' as a 'good point' and greets 'you betrayed us' as 'wonderful news,' suggesting he's on the phone and not listening to Jack.
jokes.explanation: The disconnected phone conversation running parallel to Jack's serious confrontation is a solid structural joke. The inappropriate responses ('wonderful news' to a betrayal accusation) work through the confusion.

jokes.text: God, these acoustics in here are fantastic. / Tomorrow, tomorrow, I love you, tomorrow / It's only a day away.
jokes.setup: Gavin has apparently retreated to the bathroom while Jack waits.
jokes.punchline: Gavin discovers the bathroom acoustics and spontaneously breaks into 'Tomorrow' from Annie — apparently this is a regular comfort behavior.
jokes.explanation: The image of this ruined billionaire singing Annie in the bathroom while his would-be investor waits is a lovely absurdist character moment. 'These acoustics are fantastic' as his immediate concern is funny in its priorities.

jokes.text: Well, what would this country be if our economy didn't allow wealthy people to take advantage of rubes?
jokes.setup: Jack feels guilty about losing Kenneth's money and wants to give him his own.
jokes.punchline: Jack frames exploitation of the naive by the wealthy as a foundational American institution — and says it with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: One of Jack's best lines of the episode — 'take advantage of rubes' presented as American economic heritage is sharp, dark satire in perfect Jack register. The casual use of 'rubes' to describe Kenneth is simultaneously insulting and affectionate. High character integration and economy.

jokes.text: We Parcells have eaten our share of rock soup and squirrel tail. But we've also known lean times.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is declining Jack's money, saying they'll get by.
jokes.punchline: He describes rock soup and squirrel tail as their regular diet, then characterizes THAT as the good times — implying 'lean times' are even worse than subsisting on rocks.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding Kenneth Parcell mythology-building joke. The inversion — rock soup and squirrel tail are presented as the GOOD times, with lean times being worse — is structurally elegant and very funny. 'Squirrel tail' specifically (not squirrel meat, but the tail) is a perfect detail suggesting they ate the least-desirable part. Among the episode's top jokes.

jokes.text: I need someone to be our floor emergency marshal. / And you came to me first? Thank you, sir!
jokes.setup: Liz approaches Kenneth about the emergency marshal position she can't fill herself.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's touching, grateful response — 'You came to me first?' — reveals he's so accustomed to being overlooked that any offer of responsibility moves him.
jokes.explanation: A sweet Kenneth character moment. The joke is in his eagerness for any recognition, but it's more of a setup beat for what follows than a strong standalone joke.

jokes.text: Doesn't that responsibility come with a $4,000 signing bonus? / Uh... Yes? / Oh, right, I remember that meeting. Where you also said I would get a per diem for gas. / Yes, yes, um... 12 cents a mile. / YES! HORNBERGER!
jokes.setup: Kenneth is grateful to be offered the floor emergency marshal role. He then begins negotiating.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth — gentle, naive Kenneth — cons Pete into a $4,000 signing bonus and a gas per diem for a volunteer safety position, manipulating Pete's uncertainty through fake memory of a meeting.
jokes.explanation: A masterful convergence of two plot threads. Kenneth — revealed to have hidden depths — essentially runs a long con on Pete to recover his exact $4,000 loss, escalating to the triumphant 'YES! HORNBERGER!' The callback is perfectly engineered. Kenneth's hidden sharpness is a great character reveal. One of the episode's top structural moments.

jokes.text: Daddy? / It begins.
jokes.setup: Tracy hears his son call for him from his supposedly empty bedroom.
jokes.punchline: 'It begins' — Tracy's ominous, over-dramatic response to a child's completely innocent call.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — 'It begins' is two words that encapsulate Tracy's paranoia and the Menendez Brothers subplot simultaneously. The melodrama of the response to a child's 'Daddy?' is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: Daddy? ... It begins.
jokes.setup: Tracy has set up the sex doll as a murder decoy and is waiting.
jokes.punchline: One of his sons tentatively calls 'Daddy?' and Tracy, hiding, solemnly intones 'It begins.' — treating the child's innocent call as the opening of an assassination attempt.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical joke. 'It begins.' — two words delivered with the gravity of a military commander — applied to a child saying 'Daddy?' is a perfect ratio of absurdity to economy. Very quotable.

jokes.text: I dreamed that you would get so rich that you would leave us and get a new family. And never come back. And daddy... I don't want you to leave us. 'Cause I love you. I love you so much. / I love you too, son! / Stop it. Stop patriciding!
jokes.setup: Tracy's son has an emotional nightmare about abandonment.
jokes.punchline: Tracy, instead of being moved by his son's genuine love, screams 'Stop patriciding!' — a word he invented, using it to mean any expression of love he finds suspicious.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation of the Menendez running gag. 'Patriciding' as a verb Tracy invents and uses to dismiss his son's genuine emotional expression is both funny and surprisingly dark. The son's speech is tender, which makes Tracy's paranoid rejection of it funnier. High character integration.

jokes.text: It's me. There's nothing to be freaked out about. That's just some Japanese sex doll in daddy's bed. Now, you listen. You don't have to ever worry about me leaving. 'Cause I'll always be there to take care of you. And there's something else. If anything ever happens to me, you and your brother are going to go to jail.
jokes.setup: Tracy reassures his son after the emotional appeal.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's tender speech culminates in the threat/warning that if he dies, his sons go to jail — a touching moment ruined by its dark logic.
jokes.explanation: The speech is structured as a real emotional father-son moment, making the pivot to 'you're going to go to jail' land much harder. The sex doll mention early in the speech is a beautiful reminder of the absurdity. Both touching and darkly funny — great dual-register writing.

jokes.text: Also everything worked out with Jenna's dad visiting. / What? / Oh, you weren't really around for any of that.
jokes.setup: Tracy cheerfully updates Liz on the resolution of a subplot.
jokes.punchline: The show acknowledges an entire B-plot (Jenna's dad) that Liz — and the audience — completely missed.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully meta joke — the show acknowledges that an entire storyline happened off-screen and Liz (and the viewer) missed it. This is 30 Rock at its most self-referential, treating its own episode structure as a punchline. 'You weren't really around for any of that' is a perfect curtain line.

jokes.text: Cheap cholesterol medicine from Canada. A Paris Hilton film released only in Canada. Camp of Approval? What does that even mean?
jokes.setup: Gavin tries to prove he was actually in Canada by showing evidence.
jokes.punchline: His Canadian proof includes a Paris Hilton film only released in Canada ('Camp of Approval') — an absurdist invented title that captures Canada's pop culture status.
jokes.explanation: 'Camp of Approval' as an invented Paris Hilton Canada-only film title is a nice specific absurdist detail. The Canadian exceptionalism joke is mild but the invented title adds a layer of craft.

jokes.text: Toronto was just like New York, but without all the stuff.
jokes.setup: Gavin is trying to sell Liz on coming to Canada with him.
jokes.punchline: 'Without all the stuff' — the most crushing possible description of Toronto as New York-minus-everything-interesting.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy — 'without all the stuff' does maximum work in minimum words. It's a cruel but precise description that captures a specific New York attitude toward Toronto. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: I thought by now you'd be some place that U.S. law couldn't touch you, like Bali or Utah.
jokes.setup: Jack is surprised to see Gavin back in the building.
jokes.punchline: Jack's list of places beyond U.S. legal reach: Bali (legitimate) and Utah (absurd — Utah is very much subject to U.S. law).
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist joke with perfect economy. 'Like Bali or Utah' — the inclusion of Utah as a rogue jurisdiction is an inspired, specific choice that implies Jack's view of Utah as a law-unto-itself theocracy. The joke works because it's specific and surprising.

jokes.text: You've already done enough damage, taking advantage of her loneliness and her Big Ben-sized biological clock.
jokes.setup: Jack dismisses Gavin's claim that he came back for Liz.
jokes.punchline: 'Big Ben-sized biological clock' — a hyperbolic but specific metaphor for Liz's age-related relationship anxiety.
jokes.explanation: A good metaphor with strong economy. 'Big Ben-sized' is a specific and evocative choice that elevates it above a generic 'ticking clock' joke. Jack saying this reveals both his protectiveness of Liz and his bluntness.

jokes.text: It's over, Volure. Give me the brush. / You stay back. I swear I will paint you. / I am not going to real prison.
jokes.setup: Gavin has apparently grabbed a paintbrush during the confrontation.
jokes.punchline: 'I swear I will paint you' — the threat of being painted as a form of violence from a desperate man. Also 'I am not going to real prison' implying his current arrangement is not 'real' prison.
jokes.explanation: 'I swear I will paint you' is a gloriously absurd threat. The escalating desperation of Gavin using art supplies as a weapon while insisting on the distinction between house arrest and 'real prison' is excellent character comedy.

jokes.text: I can't believe I'm saying this to the great Gavin Volure, but Liz Lemon is too good for you.
jokes.setup: Jack is defending Liz against Gavin.
jokes.punchline: The 'I can't believe I'm saying this' framing acknowledges that Liz Lemon being 'too good' for a Harvard-educated billionaire is objectively absurd — Jack is aware of the comedy even as he commits to the sentiment.
jokes.explanation: A solid character beat that captures the Jack-Liz relationship. The acknowledgment of how implausible the statement is makes it funnier and more sincere simultaneously.

jokes.text: I've lost everything. I'm financially ruined, I've lost Liz. That paint is drying weird, and now prison?
jokes.setup: Gavin lists his losses before threatening to jump.
jokes.punchline: Between losing his fortune and losing Liz, he notes that 'that paint is drying weird' — an absurdly small aesthetic concern inserted into a list of life catastrophes.
jokes.explanation: The bathos of inserting a minor art concern into a dramatic lament is expertly timed. 'That paint is drying weird' between 'I've lost Liz' and 'prison' is a perfect comedic interpolation.

jokes.text: All right, everyone, I'm in charge. Does anyone need water or saltines?
jokes.setup: A potential jumper situation has developed. Kenneth, as the new floor emergency marshal, steps up.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's emergency response plan is to offer water and saltines — the mild, unhelpful comfort foods of a church social rather than a crisis response.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the floor emergency marshal subplot is perfectly Kenneth — his emergency response is hospitality. Saltines as a crisis provision is a beautifully specific detail. High character integration.

jokes.text: I would feel safer with some saltines.
jokes.setup: Kenneth offers saltines as emergency crisis supplies.
jokes.punchline: Someone sincerely requests the saltines — treating them as legitimate comfort in a crisis.
jokes.explanation: A good button on Kenneth's saltines joke — someone earnestly requesting them validates Kenneth's crisis plan. Good economy.

jokes.text: Glenn ate all my peanut butter.
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to talk Gavin down from the ledge, listing his hardships.
jokes.punchline: Gavin adds the peanut butter grievance to his list of tragic losses.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback economy. The Glenn peanut butter dispute, which was a minor joke in the earlier scene, returns here as a legitimate grievance during a crisis negotiation. The bathos of it being in the same weight class as financial ruin is funny. 'Glenn ate all my peanut butter' as a near-suicidal complaint is a great escalation.

jokes.text: Gavin, I'm not going to lie to you, you'll probably be killed in the first six months of prison. But that's neither here nor there.
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to talk Gavin off the ledge.
jokes.punchline: Jack's crisis negotiation includes a frank admission that Gavin will likely be murdered in prison — then waves it off as irrelevant to his main point.
jokes.explanation: A superb Jack joke. The structure is near-perfect: sincere opening concession ('you'll probably be killed'), the brutal specificity ('first six months'), and then the breezy pivot ('but that's neither here nor there'). Only Jack would include a murder prediction in a suicide prevention speech and then move on. Among the episode's best.

jokes.text: Yes, you have to pay for the things you've done. / You're not making sense anymore.
jokes.setup: Jack continues his negotiation, saying there's hope.
jokes.punchline: Gavin accepts 'there's hope' but rejects 'you have to face consequences' — his moral framework only incorporates the optimistic half of Jack's speech.
jokes.explanation: A competent character joke — Gavin's selective acceptance of Jack's advice is funny and characterful. Gets the job done without being exceptional.

jokes.text: Now, Tracy! / What? But you're down there. / Or am I?
jokes.setup: Jack signals Tracy as part of a plan involving the sex doll.
jokes.punchline: The sex doll is on the ledge with Gavin — Tracy (or the doll) delivers 'Or am I?' — a callback to Tracy's earlier use of the phrase.
jokes.explanation: The sex doll plan from earlier pays off in the crisis resolution, with a nested callback to Tracy's 'Or am I?' catchphrase. The visual of the sex doll on the ledge as a tactical deployment is absurdist brilliance. Rewatch value high.

jokes.text: Good job, sex doll.
jokes.setup: The sex doll has apparently helped resolve the Gavin standoff.
jokes.punchline: Jack professionally compliments the sex doll on its performance.
jokes.explanation: Four words of maximum economy. Jack Donaghy professionally acknowledging the sex doll's contribution with no irony or discomfort is perfectly in character. The straight delivery of a completely absurd line is a 30 Rock specialty.

jokes.text: He miscounted the men.
jokes.setup: The crisis has resolved, presumably because a marshal was misled.
jokes.punchline: Liz's flat callback to Gavin's panicked earlier phrase — now delivered as a quiet post-crisis assessment.
jokes.explanation: A callback that works on multiple levels — repeating Gavin's panicked earlier line in Liz's deadpan voice completely transforms it. The understatement sells it. Perfect economy.

jokes.text: You know, a lot of people look down on sex dolls. But as we saw tonight, they save lives and bring families together.
jokes.setup: Tracy delivers an epilogue reflection on the episode's events.
jokes.punchline: Tracy summarizes the sex doll's contributions earnestly, as if delivering a PSA.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's sincere PSA about sex dolls bringing families together is both a callback curtain and a parody of Very Special Episode moral wrap-ups. The earnest delivery of an absurd thesis is signature Tracy.

jokes.text: How am I such an expert? I'm Tracy Jordan's sex doll.
jokes.setup: Tracy (or the doll) seems to be continuing the PSA.
jokes.punchline: The sex doll speaks, identifying itself — a completely absurdist fourth-wall-adjacent moment where the merchandise becomes a character.
jokes.explanation: The sex doll as its own narrator/character is an unexpected and funny escalation of the gag. The reveal that it's speaking independently (or is it Tracy?) is a meta-absurdist button on the entire subplot. High rewatch value as the episode's final joke.

tmdb_overview: Jack and Liz make a visit to a colorful businessman named Gavin Volure, who has a confidential business proposal...and has fallen in love with Liz. Meanwhile, Tracy is afraid that his kids may have figured out an evil plot against him.
insight: 75 jokes in 22 minutes makes this 30 Rock's densest episode yet.
